doc.title: Dianne Reeves interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, October 13, 2001

title: Music without boundaries: from Coltrane to Leonard Cohen
summary: She sees all music as one, with a jazz foundation allowing her to sing varied songs that address her life.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Yeah. Well if we were to look at your list of songs from this evening, you went from John Coltrane to singing that Leonard Cohen was it? But they all sound like they seemed to mesh together really well.

It’s all music to me. I’ve always believed that music should be without boundaries. And for me jazz, having a foundation in jazz music really kind of allowed me to be a part of different kinds of music, much like the musicians that were performing, or that created this fusion music. And I just felt that if you could take the popular tunes of the 40s and turn them into jazz standards then there was a possibility that with these new other forms of these other songs, or even songs that I write could even have a kind of jazz sensibility. So I wanted to sing the songs that really addressed my life early on, that really meant something deeply to me. And so that’s how all of those kinds of songs came into being.
